patch_description:
The original program failed validation: its recursive value-grouping reorder produced inconsistent DataFrames and column orderings (it fabricated an "original_index" column, mutated cell placement via `result_df.update(group)`, returned `[]` as column_orderings, and merged/dropped columns, breaking shape/row-identity requirements). The root cause was a broken recursive algorithm that didn't preserve data or return valid per-row column orderings.

I replaced the editable block with a correct, bounded algorithm aligned with the actual objective (character-Trie prefix reuse):
- Keep the DataFrame's shape, rows, and cell values exactly; only permute cells within each row and report per-row column orderings.
- Honor col_merge by treating merged column groups as contiguous units (adjacency in each row's ordering), without altering values.
- Build up to three cheap candidate orderings: (1) global frequency-ranked ordering using sum(len(v)*count*(count-1)) per column, (2) a recursive conditional partition tree selecting the best length-weighted repetition column per group with depth/work bounds, (3) a deterministic alphabetical fallback.
- Score each candidate by the true serial-Trie objective: serialize rows, sort, sum adjacent longest-common-prefix lengths (binary-search LCP so comparisons run in C). Pick the best.
- Return the DataFrame with per-row permuted values (object dtype) plus a per-row column-ordering list consistent with the returned data, rows in original order.
